item.title: Nims Dai
item.description:
In 2016, I found myself sitting between the legs of a man called Yanick. He was Belgian. He was charming (but that’s not how I found myself between his legs) and to speak, he had to shout in my ear. I was scared. Because we were on a small propeller plane, gathering altitude over Diani trying to attain the height of 10,000 ft from which I could jump. Or we could jump. With Yanick. There were two girls in the plane who would do solo jumps. Pros. They grinned at me, at the discomfort of finding myself seated between a man’s legs. My fear amused them. I was the only one who was terrified. Terrified of the position I found myself in life – between a man’s legs, obviously – but also terrified of heights. Of sitting on the floor of a small plane with its doors open, seeing the clouds, looking down and seeing how suddenly everything was so small, the beach so wide, white and frothy and thinking God sure has a nice view.

Yanick – a skydiving instructor – was mad. At 6,000 feet – to distract me from my fear, for now my hands were shaking slightly – he shouted in my ear. “Do you feel that?” I felt a small prodding on my lower back and prayed that it was one of his many hooks.

I turned back and shouted, “Yeah, but barely.”

He laughed and said, “But it’s hard and nice, isn’t it?”

The ladies – used to his insanity – roared with laughter. The plane tilted upwards. I wanted to throw up with terror. It was a trip sponsored by Tembea Kenya and Chevrolet’s Trailblazers. I don’t know why I had volunteered to jump. No, I know, it was for a story I was writing. There were turtles involved. Najib Balala – the then CS for Tourism – had jumped moments before I did. If Najib Balala could jump off a plane, surely, so should I regardless of the fact that I am terrified of heights. I could never stand too close to the edge of a balcony of a very high building and look down. My heart races and my head swims. So going up the plane seemed like a romantic idea but now, heading up felt stupid.

Yanick made – shouted – small talk. He has had over 1000 jumps, had been jumping for 15 years. He was also a pilot by profession and a member of Kenya Sky Divers Association. He frequently jumped with his girlfriend, who was Rwandan. Over the roar of the bird, she squealed, “She figured a long-distance relationship would be exciting.” Then howled in laughter. “But I also jump with my mother, she is 60!”

“Do you also poke her in the back with your little friend back there?” I asked.

The plane chortled.

“Of course!” Yanick said. “Nobody gets special treatment here, buddy.” 

More laughter. 

At 9,000 ft, planet Earth looks like an abstract painting done by a kindergarten kid. The sea dominates to the left, and to the right land spreads out defiantly. A silver necklace of white beach separates the two, looking like an accessory. Yanick pulls and tugs and tightens and secures our suit as our little bird starts doing a small curve against the azure sky. “Girls are the best people to jump with!” he shouts as he double-checks our suits.

“Why? Because they scream your name?”

“No, they never scream my name. They are always screaming some other guy’s name! You might know this guy, he’s called God.” 

I laugh. “Yes, I think I might have heard of him.”

He then imitates a screaming girl, “Ooooh my GOOOOOOOD!”

I often think humour is the closest cousin fear has. One keeps the other company. Soldiers joke. Surgeons joke. Men climbing impossible mountains joke. Divers joke. People waiting outside operating theatres joke. We laugh because the alternative is to sit quietly with the terrifying possibility that this thing might actually happen.

At 10,000ft, we sit at the edge of the door, and he says, “Deep breaths now, Jackson. Deep breaths.” I’m shaking like a leaf. I’m telling him, “Hang on a second. Just wait a minute. Just one second.” He says. “We have had many seconds, Jackson, this is it. Remember the exit is key. Hold strap, elbows out, neck stretched back on his shoulder, and knees always bent between my legs. When we jump, I want you to relax, don’t fight it, just relax your body. When you feel me tap your shoulder, I want you to let go of your harness.” 

The ladies shout, “Good luck, boys!” 

Yanick taps me on the shoulder, and suddenly we are off the plane and plunging towards earth.

And my first thought, “I’m never doing this shit ever again.” 

Which, in hindsight, is a sentence I’ve said at least three memorable times in my life. Fear, I’ve discovered, has terrible memory. In the middle of an ordeal you swear blood oaths. Never again. You say it while bent over a mountain trail, while floating beneath the sea, after a brutal run, after heartbreak, after food poisoning. Then life wanders by with another ridiculous invitation, curiosity taps you on the shoulder, and before long you’re zipping up another jacket, signing another indemnity form, introducing yourself to another stranger with questionable hobbies. Fear leaves the body much faster than curiosity does.

Which was a lie because it was also the same thought that I had when I summited Point Lenana in Mt Kenya eight years earlier in 2008. I’m from the lake – I come from a long line of fishermen – I have no reason to climb mountains, but the allure of a good story is always a great temptress. We had trekked from Naro Moru route from Point Lenana, camped at the Met Station on night one (3050m), walked throughout a rainy and wet day, eating cold sandwiches and keeping our head low, until we set camp for the night at Mackinder’s camp (4200m), which was colder than a devil’s left nipple.

I remember very little conversation from that second day. Mountains have a way of commanding silence. Everybody retreats into themselves. You become aware of strange things: the rhythm of your own breathing, the weight of your backpack, the sound trekking poles make against rock, the annoying optimism of the guide who keeps saying, “one step at a time, focus on the one step,” as though slowly somehow makes gravity lighter. Your world shrinks to the pair of boots in front of you. You follow those boots because thinking too far ahead is exhausting. Thinking too far back is pointless. Mountains teach you to live in increments of the next twenty steps.

Then the following day at 3 am we set off in the night, torches on our forehead, towards a devilish, windy, and freezing darkness to find our way to the summit. I had a constant headache from altitude sickness. I felt nauseous. I was weak and tired and miserable. And I was sleepy. Very sleepy. I told the guide, please, let me rest my head upon this boulder for one second but he wouldn’t hear of it because I heard if you sleep you die.

I don’t know about you, but there is something deeply lonely about climbing in darkness. Your torch illuminates only a small patch of earth and the heels of the hiker in front of you. Beyond that there is nothing. No mountain. No horizon. No stars worth admiring; you are floating in a yawning chasm. Your head hurts. There is only darkness and breathing. Somebody coughs. Somebody lies and says, “I’m okay.” We were all pretending, each in our own way, that we belonged up there. We don’t. Nobody belongs up those mountains, except God. And the devil. 

When we summited, I had nothing left in me. The dominant emotion I had was deep misery. I flopped on the cold rock. God, it was cold! I looked up at the Kenyan flag and remember thinking, “The flag is made from metal! Metal!” Not even the flag was real. While people took photos and hugged and looked around saying things like, “this is so stunning! This is God’s work!” I remember thinking, “I will never come up this far again to see any of God’s work.”

People imagine summits are euphoric. They imagine triumphant music swelling in the background while eagles circle dramatically overhead. They imagine tears. Hugs. Revelation. That’s not what I remember. Your lips are cracked. Your head feels like somebody is tightening bolts inside your skull. Your fingers feel like sticks. You stand there because that’s what you’ve spent two days trying to do. Then, almost immediately, somebody says, “Okay, let’s descend.” And secretly, you’re relieved because descending sounds wonderfully like going home.

But then not long after, a few years later, I went scuba diving, and I remember how dark below the ocean was. How I wanted to cough and didn’t know I could cough in my regulator, and I panicked because I’m not a fish, I have no business being in a dark, cold ocean. Underwater is perhaps the closest thing to visiting another planet without ever leaving Earth. Sound behaves differently. Time behaves differently. Even your own breathing no longer belongs to you. You inhale. A loud hiss. You exhale. A stream of bubbles races past your face. It is impossible not to become aware of your own mortality. The deeper we went, the more the sea stopped pretending to like us. Colours disappeared one by one. Reds vanished first. Then oranges. Fish glided past us confidently, creatures who had evolved exactly for this place, barely acknowledging the awkward mammals invading their neighbourhood in rubber suits. 

I remember thinking that every environment has its rightful owners. Birds own the sky. Fish own the sea. The mountain belongs to itself. We merely rent these places for a few nervous hours. And you ask yourself what compels people to do such unnatural things. The easier answer is to “feel alive.” But then sometimes when I have eaten some good chapo and beans I really feel alive. But that is never enough. Perhaps “feeling alive” is too lazy an explanation. We all feel alive in ordinary ways. Watching your child sleep. Falling in love. Eating too many mandazis than you should. Those things make you feel gloriously alive too. Yet there exists a peculiar tribe of men and women who insist on borrowing danger to sharpen that feeling. They climb into the sky. They descend beneath oceans. They sleep on cliffs. They run across deserts. They run ultramarathons. [Nick/ Bhavesh] They push and push to feel something beyond pain.

Men will do wild things.

They will face nature. And nature is a force that disregards man.

Nature is wonderfully indifferent. It doesn’t hate us. Mountains don’t wake up plotting our demise. Oceans don’t hold grudges. Avalanches aren’t angry. They simply are. That, perhaps, is what makes them so frightening. You cannot negotiate with indifference.

Consider the sound of an avalanche, which I was Googling the other night. What does an avalanche sound like? Like the earth splitting in half. Like hell at your feet. I went on YouTube to listen to recorded sounds. I read accounts of people who survived avalanches. It led me to Reddit. And then to articles written by men and women who have gone up treacherous mountains, 8000m up, in deep snow and rock and death.

The internet has made voyeurs of all of us. You go looking for one thing and end up somewhere entirely different. You search for the sound of an avalanche and, forty minutes later, you’re reading up on hypothermia written decades ago. One link becomes another. Before long you’re lying in your warm bed long after midnight, reading about people freezing to death on mountains whose names you can’t pronounce, wondering what exactly it is you’re searching for. Information is a strange forest. You enter looking for berries and somehow find a naked woman holding an apple.

I stumbled on a brilliant article on Outside by Peter Stark on how it feels like to freeze to death. I learnt that there is no precise core temperature at which the human body perishes from cold. Somehow I found myself reading about the Holocaust at the Nazi death camps of Dachau (which I visited seven years ago because I like light but I’m seduced by darkness), where Nazi doctors, experimenting with cold-water immersion baths, calculated what temperatures hypothermia occurred.

I could have easily put away my phone and continued watching the white walkers on Game of Thrones but instead I read about a two year old in Saskatchewan (that can only be in Canada) who wandered out of her house into minus 40 degrees and was found near her doorstep the following morning, limbs frozen solid, her body temperature having dropped to 13.9 degrees.

She lived.

Nims didn’t.

And that’s the only reason I was reading this stuff. Because of Nirmal “Nims Dai” Purja. 

I was reading about this stuff because I had gone on Instagram and saw on my friend Martha’s status that she was praying for the safety of some ten mountaineers who had been swept away by an avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak. Nims was one of them, a celebrity Nepali mountaineer. I had never heard of him for the life of me, but I like such stories. So I started reading about him. Then I discovered his documentary on Netflix called 14 Peaks; Nothing is Impossible and thought, “this is bloody extraordinary.” It’s a bit like that story of the Tham Luang cave rescue in Thailand in 2018, when twelve boys entered the caves, left their bicycles outside and disappeared into the darkness, the monsoon rains having flooded the inner caves barring entrance. The whole world began looking for them from their living rooms, offices, airports and cafés. Nations tweeted and prayed. Hundreds of rescuers. Cave divers from around the world. Thai Navy SEALs. Engineers. Volunteers. Prayer warriors. They searched for these children they had never met. And we read about those caves and how extraordinary they are. They found the kids nine days later. 

The world hoped Nims Dai and his team would make it.

His Garmin device continued transmitting location updates. His battery was dying. He was dying. The weather was too rubbish to attempt a rescue without risking more lives.

His battery eventually died.

And Nims died too. 

It was tragic. 

Heartbreaking. 

But also strangely beautiful. 

Not because he died. 

Of course not because he died. 

But because he had spent his life pursuing something that demanded everything from him. There are men who measure a life by its length. Others like him measure it by its intensity. It’s a thing of beauty, a thing to be admired, sometimes from far. I did all those stupid things, even after repeatedly telling myself I wouldn’t again, not because of courage, or the danger, but because of the story that awaited on the other side of it. Maybe that’s the real addiction; the narrative. The hope that somewhere beyond discomfort, beyond fear, beyond common sense, there might be a story worth bringing home. 

RIP Nims Purja.

item.title: A Report In An Envelope
item.description:
It’s so dry in the village. The live hedge fence looks like someone tried to boil it alive. There are patches of dead grass. And there is nothing as sad as dead grass. Cut grass is great, though. Smells good, even though it’s dead. But grass that died because there wasn’t enough water is deeply saddening.

I didn’t expect the wrath of the weather, but I expected this effect. The sprinklers we installed five years ago have done their time. Almost all are broken. The submersible pump sputtered, rolled over, and died. The trees grew big and covered the solar panels, which meant that even if the pump worked, it wouldn’t be getting enough power. And because nobody sane cuts trees anymore, the panels have to be moved.

A little spanner in this works. The guy, the welder guy, who is very good at what he does, is a very talented but raging alcoholic. The last time he came to work, he did a shoddy job because he was completely shitfaced, and I called him and we had a very toxic conversation over the telephone. I was mad. He was drunk.

I know he is drunk because he only speaks English when drunk. And he insists on using very complex vocabulary, most of which I have never heard of, and I have heard plenty.

So that last time, the conversation ended when I told him to get his raggedy ass out of my compound immediately before I call the chief on him, and he said, and I quote:

“I don’t have time for your indefensible tomfoolery and fundamentally sequa-angowa. Goodnight.”

I hung up and laughed. Not because of the words, but because he had seen it fit to tell me goodnight at 11 am. He was sending me to bed.

Anyway, here we are, bearing the wrath of the Nyanza sun, and everything is perishing under its glare. And here I find myself, standing at the very precipice of great humility.

I need to save my grass. I need new sprinklers. I have a new pump, and I need to move the solar panels. And I need Omollo.

He really is the best.

So I ate humble pie and called him. I prayed he was sober.

He picked up.

[Insert Luo accent.] “Biko, my nemesis. You live?”

“I live, Omollo. Chal nade?”

“Chieng rieny dala ka seriously.” He was complaining about how hot and dry it is. “Miya tich, ba.”

He wants to work.

Good sign.

Everything all forgotten.

The rule is, you don’t send him money to buy materials. He will pass by Min Phiona’s and have something first. I don’t mind him having something first, maybe that’s why he is good. The problem is if he has many of those somethings first.

Let’s see how that goes.

Anyway, my online writing mentorship masterclass mentee is “graduating” now. We have spent the last month and change writing together. She can now push her boat of words out into the ocean and find her island. I am sharing something she wrote.

By Armella Gahimbare 

Phil sat at his desk, legs spread, leaning back in his leather chair. His new suit was a little tight and his pants rode up, but that didn’t bother him. He would buy another one. Now that he was the chef de cabinet, there was no limit to what he could do. His efforts during the campaigns for the party had finally paid off. He was appointed as the right hand of the minister of health. He knew nothing about health, except the fact that it was a gold mine, and he was about to be the most successful and influential man from Mwaro, and unlike his village mates, his wealth would not come from selling beer. He had begun receiving calls from people he had not spoken to in years, as well as people he didn’t know. People in power too reached out. Everyone seemed to have his number now. He spent a lot of time on the phone, and it had been only a few months since his appointment.

The minister’s office was adjacent to his. Dr Joseph, the minister, was from Bururi of course, because that was the order of things. Phil was just fortunate that they had remembered him. Usually a guy from his neck of the woods did not sit in an office like this. The doctor would bring credibility, and he would mind politics, do the real work. They formed a good pair. Phil had already calculated that he would be able to complete his house in the next year if he worked diligently. His wife wanted to open a shop. With politics, you never knew when the tide would turn. He wanted to make the most of it while he could, give favors to those who would remember him when he was gone, investing in his own future.

Essie walked into his office carrying the mail, her heels clicking loudly. She was the secretary and acted as if she was the minister herself. Phil had found her pitched voice annoying the moment he arrived. But he needed her; she had seen a lot of ministers come and go, and bringing in someone new would not be smart. The mail was opened and classified according to priority. Essie spoke to Phil about each item, bringing him up to speed, connecting the dots. The transition between the previous cabinet and the current one had been nonexistent. The outgoing team had been bitter and reluctant to share information. Thankfully, Essie was doing a lot of that. Phil was mostly interested in international conferences, high-level meetings that came with fat per diems. There was a pile of mail that kept growing every day; it was in English, and no one in the office cared to touch it. Most of it had the colorful East African Community emblem stamped on it.

“We received more mail from EAC, and the ministry of external affairs is asking that we respond as soon as possible,” Essie said, laying out the mail on his desk.

“Call the kid we just hired. She can look at these.”

Moments later, the office messenger stood awkwardly in the doorway while his shadow fell across the dusty floor of my small office. It was so hot in the room, I kept both the door and the windows ajar, which was open invitation to all the dust that flew in from outside every time the wind blew.

From the way he hesitated, I could tell the man did not know my name and was now wondering what to call me. I looked too young to be called Madam. He finally opted for a general greeting and said I was needed in the cabinet. Finally, I thought. I was bored out of my mind, spending hours reading and doodling, waiting for the day to end. I was not the only one, though. A lot of people were idle. People hung around “waiting for work.” Some had given up and did not bother coming any longer. No one checked who was there or not; I suppose you could get paid even after you were dead. Work meant being given assignments, and those were handed to people who had the right “connections.”

Phil’s office was divided into two sections; a part was the salon where he received guests, brown sofas and coffee tables arranged in a circle; next to the window was the oversized desk and chair where he sat, swiveling as he spoke on the phone. He was on a call when I walked in. When I hesitated, not sure if I should stay or come back later, he waved me in and pointed to the chair opposite him.

When I sat, he pushed a pile of papers toward me. I picked them up and started reading through. Some dated from last year, invites mostly for meetings, follow-ups to previous communication. A number of them requested the appointment of a focal person for the EAC.

Phil hung up the phone and asked what the mail was about. I explained that the most pressing issue was to appoint a focal person, someone who would be the contact for the Ministry of Health and would coordinate with EAC so things didn’t fall through the cracks.

“Do they have money? I could be the focal point.” The bluntness with which he spoke didn’t surprise me. Everyone’s concern here was money. I looked at the terms of reference carefully, trying to find a way to tell him this was an administrative task and beneath him.

“Not certain about the funds, but they seem to have a lot of meetings coming up. Here is an invite for a technical meeting in Kisumu on communicable diseases,” I said, handing him a letter.

“Here is another one, this time in Arusha, happening next month.” I paused and looked at him, waiting for instructions.

All the meetings required someone with technical knowledge who spoke English. Phil came to the conclusion that he unfortunately could not go. Besides, East Africa was small potatoes. He wanted the big ones: Europe, US, Asia, after all, nobody understood what EAC was doing, or whether it would even hold together this time.

“You will be the focal person.”

“Me?”

“Yes, you. You make sure we respond to every letter and stay on top of whatever they want us to do.”

I panicked. “I’m not a doctor, most of these are technical meetings. I can do the admin stuff but cannot be the one to represent the ministry.”

Phil decided I was going to travel with the technical delegates and be their translator when needed. So I wrote the letter, the minister signed, and I became the EAC focal point. After that, everyone assumed the minister was my uncle or something. However, when the minister changed and Phil left, no one was quite sure whose niece I was anymore; everyone else had moved on, and somehow I was still there.

Dr Serge was the first person I traveled with. He was in his early sixties, a head full of white hair. He led the epidemiology and statistics department. Serge was fluent in English. However, the man did not care. He took naps during meetings, and when it was his turn to speak, I would kick him gently with my elbow to wake him up. He would open his eyes, look around, and say nothing. I died. Of shame. Wishing the ground would open and swallow me. Unfortunately, it didn’t.

That was the beginning of learning how to survive shame. It happened again and again. Some days I travelled with people who never showed to the meetings at all. Only on the last day. To collect their money. Grown-ups. I was not prepared for the level of shame I would have to endure on behalf of my country. I remember feeling comforted a few times, looking around the room and seeing an entire delegation of another country gone on a random afternoon, their little flag left alone on the table. At least I am here, I thought. Keeping my flag company.

The indifference my colleagues had was fascinating. I wondered if it was some kind of disease people caught once they started working for the government. There was a general sense of apathy. Most people seemed eager to get opportunities, and when they did, they did nothing to sustain or grow them.

When he could not go, Phil wanted to send his “friends” to these meetings, preferably those who came from his region. I often sat in his office negotiating with him: “Perhaps next time you can send him. This invite is asking specifically for the inspector general, and this person is not it.” He didn’t care what was being discussed or why. No one did. It was about which side of the country you came from and what your ethnic group was.

Eventually, Phil approved the inspector’s travel. Dr Leocadie was a stern lady with a glorious afro who wore long-sleeved white blouses with a buttoned collar. She fit the description of exactly what you would imagine an inspector to look like. She was surprised when she received the invite and came to my office to confirm it wasn’t a mistake.

I frowned. “Why would it be? The letter says inspector general, and that is you.”

She smiled, that smile you give little kids when you are touched by their innocence.

When she returned from her conference, I waited for her report, and it never came. I thought she must be busy; I would follow up with her next week. So I did. She said she was working on it. Three days later, I ran into her again in the parking lot and asked. She looked mildly annoyed. The next morning, she showed up in my office very early. She handed me a white envelope. I was confused.

“What is this?” I asked.

“The report you asked for.”

I opened the envelope to see a crisp fifty US dollar bill. I was stunned.

“What is this for?”

“It’s the report.”

I handed her back the envelope and spoke slowly, looking at her. “What we need is a real report. Written. With the objectives of the meeting, recommendations, what commitments were made, and who is accountable.”

The shock on her face would have been comic if I wasn’t so frustrated. She explained this was what they usually did, and a report meant an envelope. I said I needed the real, old-fashioned kind of report. She shook her head, said I should “never change,” and left. The report finally showed up on my desk two days later.

It was all enough to make me desperate to leave the job and the dusty office where I spent my time. I told my dad all these wild stories, and he could not believe how bad things were. One day I said I wanted to quit. I don’t like the job, I said. I feel out of place.

“Are you CRAZY?” Dad and I both turned to look at my mum, as if surprised to see her there. She never interfered in our conversations; she usually listened on the sidelines, and we would often forget she was there. Also, it was unlike her to shout.

“No one leaves a job because they are unhappy. No one. NO ONE. You hear me? And what will you do? Do you have another job?”

Of course, I was not going to quit without a clear plan. I was pursuing other things and didn’t want to jinx it by mentioning them before it was time. So I said nothing. I waited and kept my “imaginary problems” to myself.

Interestingly, people envied my situation, given that I was traveling every other month. I stayed in fancy places that I did not fully enjoy because I was too stressed. The meetings I attended gave me anxiety; I was constantly in rooms I wasn’t supposed to be in, expected to speak about things I didn’t know, while the people who were meant to represent didn’t bother showing up.

When I began paying attention to the other delegates, I noticed their reality wasn’t far from ours. The longest project we worked on was the HIV project, coordinated regionally by Dr O. The quarterly meetings were often held in Kisumu or in Naivasha. And the same faces showed up every time, which meant we got to know each other well. One day I sat next to Dr Beinomugisha, a tall, dark munyakole guy with a voice like thunder. While the meeting went on, he busied himself with calculations about the number of cement bags he needed to finish the walls of his house. Against each of the upcoming meeting dates, he wrote how much per diem he expected to receive and what that would mean for his project. He didn’t bother to hide what he was doing; he wrote his entire plan down in big letters, his massive hand moving across the paper, circling and highlighting key milestones of his construction project.

The Kenyan delegate was a flamboyant man who wore too much perfume and gold. He handed out compliments so uncomfortable they made women want to gag a little. His shoes were shiny, as if he rubbed them with Vaseline every morning. And he always had to “rush” back to Nairobi, where he was “urgently needed.” He often seemed misplaced and absent-minded, like he was supposed to be somewhere else but couldn’t remember where. His English was polished, but his arguments always gave the impression that he was having a different conversation.

It was around that time Rwanda began its rebranding crusade. I remember one day Dr Steve stood to give his presentation, and the first three slides were about their gorillas and visiting Rwanda. He said the words hesitantly, like he wasn’t convinced himself but had to do it because his government had ordered him to. We all knew the country well and we knew Steve, so his little pre-presentation amused the gallery. I could see others stifling laughter and shaking their heads. But Steve kept going. At every meeting after that, those same three slides were presented without fail, by whichever delegate from Rwanda happened to be there. They drilled it into us, visit Rwanda, until we half believed in their story and their newfound identity.

Dr Juma, the Tanzanian, was an affable man who wore kaunda suits. He bent his head on the side while speaking. Juma enjoyed his food. As always in those meetings, they overfed us like newborns on a feeding schedule, a tray showing up every two hours whether we were hungry or not. In the afternoon, Juma vanished. At lunch he would often have a whole fish with ugali, the kind of meal that puts you straight to sleep.

Aside from being the focal person, I was often asked to do live translation during official meetings for the minister. They were often courtesy visits that were meant to be light and brief but were in fact critical. Excessive gifts were often exchanged in all formats, unusual information was shared, and sometimes documents were signed.

It was then that I met Dr Kraisintu, a Thai pharmaceutical scientist and activist. She was coming to teach and support the manufacturing of affordable generic HIV/AIDS treatments and malaria drugs in the country. After the audience with the minister, I was asked to be her translator during her stay. We spent a lot of time together. It occurred to me then that wherever you see a problem in the health system, someone is benefiting from the chaos. The thousands of mosquito nets, malaria drugs, and antiretroviral drugs, whether donated or bought, meant that many hands were greased along the way. Dr Kraisintu trained people (what do you even call people who make drugs in a lab?) on how to manufacture them, but the project never took off. It wasn’t beneficial to the government; there was no money to be made. Yes, it could have saved the lives of millions who ruined themselves buying drugs they could get for free if only they were manufactured locally, but who cares? It was all shut down. Dr Kraisintu wasn’t surprised.

“It’s the same everywhere,” she said. “We can smile all we want with all these officials, at the end of the day, they are given juicy gifts every time there’s a donation or a new stock of drugs is ordered.”

Thailand was the first developing country in the world to manufacture high-quality generic ARVs at an affordable price and give free HIV medicine to its citizens. It hadn’t come easy, she fought court battles with big drug companies, received death threats, it took years but it happened. “You never know,” she said before she left. “One day things might change here too.”

I laughed. Even then, it was a long shot to imagine, and that was eighteen years ago. I wonder how much thicker the envelopes have gotten.

item.title: Where Is This Going?
item.description:
I like humans. But I don’t like people. 

When many humans gather, it changes the temperature of interactions. It gets warmer, yet I get the urge to leave. I can’t stand big dinners. Or parties. Where you have to make conversations with strangers and ask about their lives and genuinely act very interested when they tell you about the time they broke their leg for thirty minutes. There never is any reason to tell one story for thirty minutes. Even if you break two legs. One leg can get two minutes. I also hate being told what to wear to places like it usually happens where humans gather. The other day I saw a rhumba event – I love rhumba – that looked like something I would have loved to attend, but they said it’s an all-white event. 

I’m an adult. 

We are adults. 

Why must our clothes be characters for the evening? Why do we have to coordinate with other strangers? People are a committee. And committees, as we know, are where good ideas go to die.  Besides, I only ever wear black. So on top of having to deal with the anxiety of being with people, I also have to look like them? All of them?

When I was in my thirties, I used to admire men who lived in solitude. Guys who would go camping alone by a river or a lake. Once, while doing a story about some seven waterfalls in the Aberdares, we stumbled upon a man living in a wooden cabin beside a river. He was half-white, but very white in mannerisms. There was an axe leaning against the wall of his house. I wondered if he chopped wood, as solitary men do in the movies before a car shows up with a man in a suit who wants him to do just one last job. He smelled of tobacco. He told us he liked disappearing there once in a while because it allowed him to “reflect.”

I liked the very idea of it.

The romance of it.

It felt very male. To grow an itchy stubble in the woods. Your phone dead. To chop your own firewood and sit alone in a wooden house at night, a lantern burning yellow beside you, eating a meal in silence, looking both grave and peaceful, as solitary men are required to do.

I liked going down to Pinkkalelaman when it was still just a few cabins by Lake Elementaita, and Macharia would be there alone, with his dogs following him. The mountains, mute witnesses to the silence that always befell the acacia-lined shoreline. And to run into other fellows who had come there alone. Who sat by the fire, staring hard into it. Mostly older men. I’d hang around for two days and leave by Sunday. I could never stay for over four days. I gradually discovered that staying anywhere past three days alone is hounding. It felt unnatural not to talk to anyone for four days. Not to listen to a cough. To see a human smile. To feel words leave your body, directed to another human. 

I don’t understand people who go on holiday alone for a week. Solo trippers. I have seen them on game drives, sitting quietly, a Maasai shuka draped over their shoulders. Later in the evening, they sit alone at the bar, nursing a cocktail in a short glass. I have seen them by the swimming pool, napping under an umbrella, an open book covering their face from the sun. One hand dangling over the edge, the body surrendered to the death of sleep. Then later you see them eating alone at a table at dinner. Occasionally looking up and stare intently at some spot in the high, thatched roof, as they chew their food slowly. 

And at breakfast, they come in late because people who travel solo love to sleep in, or they had gone for a long solo walk on the beach. They stroll along the buffet holding a plate with nothing on it but a croissant, deciding what else to befriend the pastry with. Because a croissant is a social pastry. I always find these people fascinating. There is a particular “loneliness” to standing at a hotel buffet with one croissant on your plate.

Unless I’m on a work assignment, I’m not going on holiday alone. I’m not camping alone. I’m not chopping wood alone in a forest. I’m not staying anywhere alone for a week. It will be sexy the first three-ish days. But then, at night, the fury of loneliness will come for me. It will possess me with a kind of madness that no sentence I read, no book I hide in, can exorcise. Because who doesn’t like the sound of someone walking around in the next room? Someone to read something out loud to when you run into a sentence. Someone to turn to and say, “Listen to this.” A warm body at night. Preferably naked. Humans are nice. But not when they are many. 

I wanted to tie this idea of solitude with another thought, a segue, but I forget what that is now.

item.title: A Curse, My Foot
item.description:
When you are seven years old and your father has one arm, you never want him to come to your school. Neither do you want him to come when you are nine or twelve. Or sixteen. Actually, you don’t want him to come at all. Because your dad having one arm is a stain on your reputation, your street credibility. Because as a child, all you have is your street credibility. And you have to protect it. Otherwise, other nine-year-olds will sense this great family flaw and your life will never be the same again. You will become the boy whose father has one arm. Maybe even earn yourself a nickname. There were many causes of dying; dying from embarrassment, he felt, was always high on his list. You’d rather fall off a moving car.

“And so we were always terrified of our father showing up at school,” Mogaka tells me. “Terrified! I mean it. And my mother, oh my mother,” he laughs, shaking his head, “My mother would say, if you don’t perform well in class, I’m not coming to talk to your teacher. Your father will. So we worked hard, man. Me and my siblings. We’d do anything for him not to show up.”

His father worked for the post office. He wore a suit to work and tucked the empty left sleeve into his pocket. Sometimes the sleeve came loose, and he couldn’t be bothered to tuck it back in, so he would come home with it swinging beside him, a loose marionette of an arm.

In his other hand, there was always a cigarette burning.

“His hand was strong. His fingers thick, with dark nails from all the smoking and also because it’s the hand that did everything.”

His father never carried a wallet. Always cash. Perhaps because removing money from a wallet with one hand was too much trouble. Somehow, he read a newspaper with that hand. Polished his shoes with it. Did all the small, unremarkable things that two hands usually do without anyone thinking about them. “I don’t, for the life of me, recall how, but he would do all these things with one hand.”

To mean he never needed a hand.

Inside the house, they never noticed this disability. “It was normal. We only realised he was one-handed when we were outside, when people stared at him.”

That was the strange thing about his father: at home, he had one arm. Outside, he had one arm and an audience.

At some point, he bought a cream-coloured, left-hand-drive Citroën and drove it with that one hand. While smoking. And pointing at something. “I don’t know how legal it was for him to drive; for anybody to drive around with one arm. He was an important man in the post office, so I guess he could do anything he wanted.”

“So what happened to his hand?” I ask him.

“I don’t know,” he says.

He’s 39 now. “Surely. It must have come up,” I tell him.

“This was a long time ago, you didn’t ask your father such things. Kids nowadays will ask their parents anything, we didn’t have that licence. But we asked our mother, and she told us to mind our own business.”

I chuckle, which makes you wonder if your father’s missing arm is his business or your business.

It gets better.

“It gets better,” he tells me. “Do you know what polydactyly is?”

I tell him I don’t.

“Do you know what bilateral polydactyly is?”

“If I don’t know what polydactyly is,” I say, “surely I wouldn’t know what bilateral polydactyly is?”

The word bilateral, in my experience, has always belonged to trade agreements.

“It’s when you have extra fingers or toes,” he says. “And bilateral polydactyly is when you have extra fingers on each hand.”

He pauses, allowing the picture to form. “Your dad had extra fingers on the good hand?”

“No. My grandfather was a polydactyl.”

Hmm.

When I don’t say anything, because I am still trying to digest this, because I have not yet found the words to accompany my thoughts, he says:

“He had six fingers. On each hand.”

He says this almost proudly, as though he expects me to applaud. For him. Or perhaps for his grandfather.

“We were scared of him. Our shags is in Dagoreti, so we would go to visit him every weekend. This was a long time ago, when Dagoreti was still a village and not what it is now. He liked to carry us and toss us into the air. We’d cringe at being held with those hands, with all those fingers. Then he would chase us around, dangling those dead extra fingers at us, like you would scare a child with a dead rat or a snake or something. We’d run screaming and crying, and my dad would laugh. My mom didn’t find it so funny, but my grandfather was rich.”

He pauses.

“If I was to go on a podcast to talk about family trauma, family wounds,” he scratches the air with his fingers, making quotation marks, “like these young people. I’d talk about my grandfather’s little fingers.”

“How did your grandfather make his money?”

“I will come to that.”

His grandfather was a wealthy, polygamous man who drank a lot.

“And so my father and all his brothers took after him; they drank quite a bit. But they were not the horrible sort of drunks who stagger and beat women. They were the good type, the ones who sang and gave you money when they were drunk. A very loving bunch. My uncles lived around my grandfather and so there was always someone drunk and giving you money. We always hoped we would find him drunk because we would go back home with money. He would even give my dad and mom money. He’d say, go to my briefcase and bring some money. I was the eldest, I knew the combination of his briefcase; 03090.”

When he was sixteen, his mother told him that an old medicine man who came from the edge of a forest was displeased with his grandfather and had cursed him.

“My grandfather was a collaborator. He worked for the British. My mom told us that while all his brothers ran into the bush to fight as Mau-Mau, he chose the easy route: to work for the Man. And for that he was rewarded with lots of land around Dagoreti, Kikuyu and Karen areas. Of course he was hated for working for the mzungu. But then he got so much land and wealth he became a don of sorts. And you can hate a don, but what will you do? You have to let him touch your forehead.”

All very interesting, this don business. But I am waiting for the curse.

Instead, he lights a cigarette.

We are standing on the small balcony of his office block. He is a business owner. He’s stocky and wide on the shoulders, with a crooked hairline. It’s the first thing I noticed and wondered why nobody had ever told him that his barber isn’t doing him favours.

“So…” He puts the packet back into his jacket. “When my dad’s uncles ran away into the forest to fight these white people, and my grandfather chose this path, the medicine man gave my grandfather a warning against working for the devil. And when my grandfather refused, the medicine man told him that he would have deformities, and that his children’s children would also have deformities.”

He turns his head and blows smoke away.

“Of course, by then my grandfather had been indoctrinated by the white man against the ‘primitivity’ of his own people. Because now he was dressing in well-pressed khakis and hats and polished shoes and,” he waves his cigarette like a magician waving a cane, “he probably owned a bicycle and later a vehicle. The first person to drive a car in my lineage, just so you know. So he thought, bullshit. He was young and aggressive, a kid who wanted to get ahead. Maybe twenty-five? Anyway, we are told that not long after, his fingers started growing. And legend has it that his feet started growing extra toes too. But we never saw him shoeless. Ever. But one of my younger grandmothers apparently said the man had extra toes too.”

He turns to look at me.

I get the feeling he has told this story so many times that people usually look at him with open mouths. Or roll their eyes and say, a curse? Come on. I do neither.

Instead, I find myself wondering whether I would have been a collaborator had I lived in those times.

Or would I have run off to the bush to grow my hair, live with animals, sleep in the rain and cold, thick cold snakes crawling over my legs at night, and lug a wooden rifle that sometimes would jam, get shot at, not to see my parents or my children or my wife? Would I have chosen freedom in a world that was not free? To be hunted by imperial forces day and night, waking each morning to the possibility of death, living like an animal because the alternative was to live like a subject?

Or would I have worked for the Man?

Been a clerk. Had them send my children to school in London. Worn shoes. Shared a blanket at night with the warm body of my wife. Gone to sleep without wondering what would crawl over my leg. Not eaten rabbit barely cooked over an open fire because the imperialists were watching for smoke.

I am afraid to say how this pendulum would have swung, my dear countrymen. I hate snakes.

So I ask him, “Just how much land was your grandfather given?”

He grins.

“Well…” He brings the cigarette to his lips and draws on it. “He had a lot of land. He had seven sons and four daughters. They all had at least 20 acres each. At least. I don’t know.” He shrugs, takes another drag and then says gravely, “But a curse is a real thing.”

When he was in high school at Othaya Boys, he stepped on a thorn. Part of it broke off inside his foot. He went to the school sanatorium. “It was nothing. They removed it, and I went about my business.” But then the area began to swell. It became raw, angry red and painful to the touch.

“The foot kept swelling and getting worse, so I called my mom, and she sent my father to pick me up.”

That evening, he could hear the low, droning voices of his parents arguing in their bedroom late at night. In the morning, his mother woke him up early; dress up. We are going to see another doctor, she told him.

“Her eyes were red. She had been crying. I doubt she had slept at all.”

He was taken to KNH to see a doctor who did scans and tests and prescribed some drugs. When she dropped him back home, she had to go to work, she was a secretary at the Ministry of Finance. She prayed for him in the car.

It was one of those old Datsuns, you know, the ones with the low, smooth bums.

He did not get better.

“The pain was crazy. I’d barely sleep at night.”

They went back to see an orthopaedic surgeon. More scans. More drugs. Weeks passed.

“My foot got worse and worse, and I could barely walk. I remember my parents taking me to shags, and this very old grandmother coming to see me, must have been a medicine woman, and spitting on my foot.”

He laughs.

“You have to know my mother to know that that was wild. She is a very staunch Christian, the type that prays all the time, waking up at 3 am and all. So to take me to some old woman to rub things on my leg and spit on it?”

Anyway, he couldn’t go back to school. By the time the schools were closing, half his leg was dead, and they were seriously considering amputation.

“My parents were, at this time, fighting more and more. The house had tension. My sisters would come back from school and gather around my dead leg. Will they cut it? They’d whisper, worried but also intrigued. They would poke it with the rubber end of their pencils and ask, can you feel anything?’

One time, his father was seated with his foot on the coffee table, smoking, when his mother came to place food on the table. She snapped at him.

“She said in Kikuyu, remove your foot, what man shows off his foot while his child’s foot suffers from a curse from your family?” He nods and crushes his cigarette on the balcony slab. “Yup, the cat was out of the bag, so as it turns out, I went into the theatre one morning, and when I came out, I didn’t have a foot. I was in Form Three. Which is the worst time to lose a foot, as a teenager.”

I decided to go out on a limb and say, “But there isn’t exactly the right time to lose your foot, is there?”

“I guess,” he says moodily, “do you want to see?”

“Of course,” I tell him.

“Sawa, come.” We walk back into his office where he sits down and pulls up his trouser leg. A hard plastic cup grips the stump below his knee. A narrow metal shin runs down from it, ending in an artificial foot, the whole thing covered in a soft, flesh-coloured sheath. We stare at it. I get the feeling that I should compliment it, say something nice about this leg before us.

“It’s sexy,” I say.

He laughs.

“I get that a lot.”

We study the leg.

“I got this ten years ago. Before that, I was hobbling around on crutches. That was the worst period of my life.” I ask him questions. Do you remove it when you go to bed? Can you swim with it? Can you run with it? Is it true that sometimes you can feel the leg that isn’t there? Has it ever come off accidentally while you are, I don’t know, going up a staircase? And what is dating like with one leg? Do you declare it immediately before the starters? Er, Linda, before you embark on that Beef carpaccio, I want to say here first that I have one leg.

“Interesting, actually,” he says, laughing. “Some babes outrightly used to say, ‘No, not for me.’ It would put them off. Some thought of it as a fetish.”

“What, they’d ask you to remove it and jump around naked on one leg?”

“Oh, worse,” he laughs. “One girl I dated, this is before I got married, she had a mad temper. We once fought, and she took away my leg and ran away with it to punish me. She stayed with it for three days. Thank God I had an extra pair.”

I wonder where she hid the poor man’s foot. In the pantry, perhaps, next to the beans and rice. Under her bed. Or maybe she simply leaned it in a corner of the bathroom, like a mop.

“So what happens now?” I ask him.

“My mother prays for us, but she also took us to that medicine woman, who made small incisions in our underarms. Here,” he shows me his underarm, where there is a small scar, “she rubbed something in there. Me and my sisters. I was young, in university. She said that was to stop the curse from going down to our children.

“I have a son, and so far he is fine. No extra fingers or anything like that.” He crosses his fingers.

“One of my sisters has a daughter. Also fine.”

“What about your cousins?”

“I have many cousins. They don’t seem to have any major problems, apart from alcoholism, which is rampant in our bigger family. And one cousin is in jail for killing someone with his car.

“All these problems aren’t unique to our family. I don’t think it’s the curse, even though I suspect some of them went to see other medicine men to stop the curse. We really don’t talk about it in the family. But it’s something that is low-key. Like a taboo topic?”

Maybe the curse ended with him.

Maybe it never existed.

Maybe it is simply one of those stories families tell themselves to make sense of the things that happen to them.

Or maybe it is still waiting.

For the children.

item.title: All Men Must Die
item.description:
If you went to a concert and spent the evening watching the main artist on a giant screen, were you really at the concert? How different is that, really, from watching a YouTube video of the same artist projected onto a very large wall? It is the old tree-falling-in-the-forest adage, except the tree is Congolese with a rubbery waist and wears a very expensive jacket.

I never saw Fally in the flesh.

When he came on, most people leapt out of their seats and ran towards the stage on the regular side, where there was sustained screaming, almost geological. I remained in my seat. I felt too grown-up to run towards a stage. Too old to scream. Not for another man, at least. And certainly not a man with a naked torso, gyrating his waist. In fact, it felt too melodramatic to engage in, like trying to be the guy who knocks everything off an office desk with one sweep of his hand and hoists the woman onto it. Besides, what would be the point of paying for VIP only to abandon your VIP seat and go stand with everyone else? Apart from the fact that you get a comfortable seat and someone occasionally comes around to bring you a menu. And, crucially, your phone is considerably less likely to disappear.

A tree fell, but I was not there to hear it. But it fell. 

I’m mad at Fally. He did not play any of my favourite songs: Maria PM, Catafalque, Travelling Love, Une Minute. He didn’t play Cadenas. Chaise Electrique. Nyokalesse. Fine, these are very slow, lingering songs, but they are my slow, lingering songs, they make me escape the planet on his magic carpet. He played MayDay, which is one of the best songs we will ever be blessed with from him, but still not, in my estimation, worth the price of a VIP ticket.

But before the concert, I went to a unique book club. It was over at Zinos bar in Langata Otiende’s Trumac Square. Trumac Square sounds like a relative of Trafalgar Square, some grand European place with a gurgling fountain and pigeons flapping above it. Fortunately, it’s not. It’s a salt-of-of-the-earth local. 

I got out of the Uber holding my jacket and my hat and called Nyokabi. 

Interviewed Nyokabi here once. You can read the story HERE, it was titled Fahrt der Freiheit. She married a gay man in Germany, a wedding her boyfriend drove her to. Then married a Liberian-American man in North Carolina. Then married an American man she met in a petrol station in South Carolina. Never a dull moment with Nyokabi; brilliant, hilarious, creative and completely out-of- pocket. She is a special education teacher, runs a learning-support centre from her backyard garden, working with autistic children. Earlier in her career, she worked as an interpreter for deaf people, including interpreting for deaf women giving birth, deaf people in court, and children with mental-health problems. She is difficult to explain. How do you describe blue to someone who has only known green?

She never texts me. She sends voice notes instead – exuberant, hilarious, outrageous, and sometimes wildly incongruous – the way I like it. I call her Nyokabi FM.

She comes bundling out of the bar screeching, “My daarrrrling, you made it! Sooo exxxxxxciting” Then she hugs me and starts talking nonstop: We haven’t started yet, can you believe it? It started late. We haven’t even started discussing your book. So you are early, in that sense, even though we are late in another sense. But you can sit and listen to the discussions. Yeah? You don’t mind? The babes don’t know you are coming, maybe some suspect, but it’s been a secret so far. They will be so eexxccccciiiiited. Are you hungry? Your food is also ready. The chicken is delicious. You said with ugali, right? Like a guy, none of that chips nonsense. [Steps back dramatically] Your head is shiiiiiinnnnnny, my Gaaaaarrd! Did you shave for us? [Lowers voice] Admit it, you shaved for us. [A little girly giggle] Oh my God, this is so exciting! We have eaten, though. Do you want to go in now? We are all at the back. It’s a small group of seven babes, one is online. She [puts up a British accent] is reaching us all the way from London. You are not shy, are you? You can’t be shy, you are Jackson Biko, baby..

I’m grinning like an idiot. 

She truly is an excellent love bomber. She will hype you until you develop little bubbles of helium inside you, and before long you are floating off the ground, carried away by the wind. When I get a word in, I ask, “Where can I keep my jacket and hat? You came with your car?” She grabs my shit and rockets off towards her car out in the bustling lot. It’s 3:20pm. The sun feels particularly lower this afternoon.

The antithesis of the afternoon starts immediately when I step through the threshold of the bar.  

The air inside is cool and dark-ish; like a self-respecting bar should. Immediately to the right sits a regal, distinguished-looking woman, a little elderly, dressed so colourfully and stylishly she could have fallen out of Soweto, one of those fabulous gogos in their beautiful traditional finery. Nyokabi introduces me. “Oh yes! Welcome, please come in. Nice to meet you! Come in!” I learn that she is the owner of the joint, “Njeri and Nduta’s mom, you will meet Nduta shortly.” Nyokabi says. “Nduta is the one who chose your book.”

I tell her, “That lady has money. You can tell. Or she has handled money. A lot of money.”

She laughs.

We walk past the bar, where a television is showing some football match above us. Men at the counter sit with their backs to the room, drinking.

At the back, seated and standing around a table, is a knot of women. Nyokabi introduces me in her true Nyokabi fashion, and they all start talking at once. Nyokabi called it ‘clacking.’ 

I shake hands, exchange niceties. I know one, Sophie, whom I hug. I haven’t seen her in ages. If you hang around, you will see how Sophie later takes a saber and decapitates me, leaving my head on a spike. They speak with a kind of effortless eloquence, like people who spend a lot of time around ideas, and most with a hint of some foreign accents, which I assume means that they have spent some time living or studying abroad. 

The juxtaposition of this moment is almost startling. Out here in the back is a modest local setting, with torn tarpaulin flapping in the wind.(Ok it wasn’t, but it’s my story). A carpenter with a pencil stuck behind his ear, hammers and saws, making a bed. Every so often, a boda guy revs his bike, momentarily drowning the conversation. Whilst in here, these women speak with the aplomb of not merely the educated but the learned. It feels like the collision of two worlds in a small room; the setting says one thing; the women say another.

The energy of the room immediately reminds me of Roxane Gay’s famous book, Difficult Women; formidable, opinionated, accomplished, unconventional women who don’t seem particularly interested in making themselves smaller or more agreeable. I feel that it is going to be a tough crowd. Maybe I need a strong whisky. But I needed food, more urgently. 

On a video call is Njeri, wearing a bright yellow top and an impossible smile. She is a doctor, I learnt. 

The room has already begun to fizz. Someone is pouring a drink. There is a muted pop as a prosecco is opened. There is laughter, chiding, arguments that sound impassioned even when I can’t quite tell what they are about anymore. Curiously, for all the eruptions and interruptions, they somehow listen to one another. The hair around is eclectic, and all say something: short, dyed blonde, dreadlocked. Copper and silver accessories dangle and glint from earlobes and wrists. They carry evidence of other places, experiences, identities and worlds with them, while searching at the same time. The book club intentionally doesn’t have a name, perhaps because they believe naming things gives them an energy, and once you name it, you have already started limiting it.

One of the women, Sly, artistic, a tattoo of Mama Africa on her right arm, says, “You know, we met once. At a physiotherapist’s waiting room!”

“Oh?” I say. 

I don’t remember. But her eyes look familiar.  

“Yes, you had broken your arm!” 

I have never broken my arm. I have fallen off a bike and banged my elbow pretty badly, but I have never broken an arm. Or any other limb. Maybe the heart. But I didn’t see a doctor for that. 

“Really?” I say. 

“Yeah. In a rugby match.” 

Ohhh. I know what this is. “No, you must be talking about Steve Biko, Adema. The rugby guy?”  The table starts chiding her.

“But wait, I have met you before still,” She speaks over them, “In Sweden. We went to Sweden together, for an art trip a few years back.” Oh yes. I remember her from that trip years ago. Now the eyes make sense. She has unique contact lenses that look like she could play a Dragon mother in a fantasy movie.

There is Muthoni, whose composure suggested she was accustomed to the nuances of things. She is a lawyer, writer, political strategist and feminist, and has been recognised among the 100 most influential people in Gender Policy by Apolitico.

There is Sophie, a DNA scientist, whom I already mentioned will be my decapitator. She is tough as nails, assertive, direct, smart. She doesn’t mind drawing her sword. She doesn’t mind tearing something down to build it. Or discard it. Seated across from her is Julie, who lives in people’s heads for a living; a psychotherapist and psychosexual therapist, and runs @breakfastwithjulie on TikTok. She has a tattoo of an acacia on her arm and another line of ink tucked beneath her left underarm.  At the end of the table quietly sits Nduta, artsy and dreadlocked, the youngest of the group. She, the “baby of the group” is a sponge. She observes and listens, standing on the banks, never joining the fray. She seems to have a whole river moving inside her.

Then there is Wachuka, who works in IT. She is very quiet. Suspiciously quiet. The kind of quiet that makes you suspect there is a whole orchestra playing underneath her bonnet, only she has the good manners to keep the volume down.

The discussions begin just as my kienyeji chicken arrives. 

The traditional vegetables are excellent. 

There are only seven of them, but the whole afternoon feels as though I am in a room with forty-seven women. Forty-seven women talking about a book someone else wrote. They beat it with their little hammers of words, like people attacking a lobster, cracking the shell, pulling out the meat. How it went is each one of them took turns to pose a question that arose for them in the book, then they discussed it and then rated it. 

“Can understanding your partner’s trauma make you tolerate behaviour you shouldn’t?” [Njokabi]  “When does ‘I’m just being honest’ become emotional violence?” [Wachuka] “How much compromise is healthy before you start losing yourself?” [Njeri] “When does standing your ground become an unhealthy need to be right?” [Sylvia]  “Do we tell relationship stories to understand the truth – or to make ourselves look right?” [Muthoni] “How do you know when you’re fighting for a relationship versus fighting against reality?” [Sophie, the decapitator] “If you had to challenge one fundamental idea in this book, what would it be?” Nduta – Mine “Are the ‘little fights’ actually the problem- or simply symptoms of bigger problems we refuse to confront?” I got great ratings from the rest; mostly 8/10, maybe one 7/10 or so. 

“I struggled with this book!” Sophie said. The characters annoyed her. “They were all juvenile!” If she was in her younger twenties, the book would have worked for her, she says. “Foolish individuals,” she hissed. “That girl who was driving like a maniac because the boyfriend left her? Oh my God, what was that? I hope they died, all of them…” 

Thank God, by this time I had finished eating my kienyeji chicken, which made me remember the famous Luhya proverb; whatever happens, eat first. 

She went on. She found the characters “superficial”, the men were “simps” [Muthoni raised an objection to the word] “they aren’t manly!” and, when someone asked, I don’t remember who, “are men meant to be manly?” She shot back, “For me, yeah!”

But it’s not only the man she had a problem with. She found the female characters “emotionally dysregulated.” [I was writing all these down while trying to be strong]. She shook her head and sighed and ploughed on, hacking at the book. “I don’t care what these couples wanted,” she said, “I couldn’t care about what they were fighting about because I wasn’t invested in them.” She said the characters weren’t developed enough for her to truly invest in them. It was both jarring to see a criticism of my book in real time. It was humbling. Horrifying in the moment, but deeply humbling. Particularly because this is someone I was acquainted with, so I knew her feedback came from a good place. Maybe a place with screeching sounds, but good nonetheless. 

She had taken screenshots of passages that had completely got her goat. She read them aloud, like hanging out dirty linen. There were two, but my mind, in its need to protect me, only remembers one. It’s the one at the wedding, Chapter 18.

She read it out loud,”…at the wedding I made my way towards him, treading bare feet on the grass while holding up the hemline of my wedding gown. I could tell the colour of the grass by just stepping on it with my feet….Oh My God! How can one tell the colour of grass by…” 

She stopped herself. 

She was close to throwing her phone at me. She was truly irked by that passage. “Why?!  I could tell the colour of the grass by just stepping on it with my feet? But Why?!” She looked at me like my mother would look at me after I’d done something so bad she didn’t have it in her to beat me anymore. She was done with me. I no longer mattered. I belonged to the universe. Or my ancestors. 

“Why?” She asked me. “We will fight about this, you know that? Do you want to fight?” 

I didn’t want to fight. I wanted a drink. 

I wanted my mother. 

Anyway.  

She rated the book a three.

3/10.

A dictionary could have scored better. A recipe for boiled eggs would have scored a 5.  

My head rolled off my body and was stopped at the foot of her chair. 

Then she placed her foot on it. 

It also turned out to be her birthday, or they were celebrating her birthday because a cake was brought out and we sang for her, and she offered me a piece (an olive branch?) which I accepted because I was done with being shouted at.

I figured – in the spirit of glass half full – I might have gotten away with it easily, imagine how much worse it would have been for me if it wasn’t her birthday and she was in a less-than-good mood?

I know it might not sound like it, but I enjoyed the book club. I would go back and take it on the chin again. 

As Nyokabi walked me out after the niceties and goodbyes, she said, “This went very well, yeah? You should have been here when some female writer came for the same, it was brutal. She really had a hard time.” 

At the Tamarind Tree Hotel, I sat at the bar counter and ordered a double Lagavulin. Neat. 

I took a sip.

Then I closed my eyes.

item.title: The Long Shadow of Leaving
item.description:
Ice melted in a valley in Nepal and turned into a flood of death, carrying hundreds of people away. Whole buildings, several stories high, were swept along like cardboard model houses. The wrath of nature often veers close to the macabre.

In the Middle East, the Houthis are stirring the pot of war, fighting with a spirit unmatched. Sometimes barefoot. Skin in the game. Literally.

Meanwhile, the United Nations has recorded the highest temperatures ever for the month that passed. The earth is slowly becoming chocolate. We are turning into dessert.

You know Stella Juva, the solar-powered ambulance? Some young Dutch engineering students designed it, and it was recently tested, successfully, in Kenya. The Olympic flame has also arrived in Senegal for the Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic sporting event to be held on African soil.

Things are happening.

Oh.

There is a bird called the slaty egret. There is nothing slutty about this egret. It is dark, long-necked, and found only wading through the wetlands of Southern Africa. The bird is very sensitive to environmental disturbances and changes in its ecosystem. Recently, it was spotted in Botswana’s Okavango Delta, something that made people who are obsessed with the environment stand up, clap, and pop champagne bottles.

Closer to what I actually care about.

Tamms went off to university.

Which says so much and so little at the same time. Because most eighteen-year-olds are going off to university. It is the cycle of life, turning a road that will never meander back, passing hills and valleys, and continuing until it becomes something more important than a road.

It becomes a path.

Theirs.

Just the other day she was holding the crown of my head while I tied her shoelaces. Now she was telling me at the airport, “Papa, my boyfriend will be coming to say goodbye. Do we have time after we check in for me to go back out and hang out with him a bit?”

It was 5am. The airport was cold and busy, the fluorescent lights still burning against the dark outside. Queues meandered towards the desks, travellers pushing their lives in suitcases, their faces drawn with sleep. Air travel is a dirge in motion.

After checking in, I settled into one of the lines of chairs opposite immigration and waited as she went back outside to say her goodbyes to this boy.

She took a while.

Oh, to be eighteen and in love. To believe that the whole of the world’s love has existed in waiting for this love. Because your love is bright, shiny and pure. That you shall never seek another. Never want another. It is the purity of it that is so refreshing, so noble, before all that clarity is fogged by doubt and disappointment, before life begins rubbing its dirty self against you, like a dog that’s been rolling in the dirt.

I read a bit and, after forty minutes, texted her that she needed to come back. The queue for immigration was starting to get ugly. I got up and stood in line with her carry-on and my backpack. After a while, I saw her bobbing towards me. She’s a tall girl, so she bobs over heads and shoulders. She’d done her hair in the way I like, these massive braids that curl and twist and weigh about 300kg. She looked like a goddess wading through the crowd, all that hair rising above the heads of strangers.

“How’d that go?” I asked, trying to sound nonchalant.

“Went well. He said hi.”

“Mmm.”

“His mom brought him,” she said.

I chuckled. “Wow! At this hour?”

Lady, who had dropped us off at the airport, said that in the parking lot she had passed a small, bird-like lady in a pink sleeping robe, walking fast, visibly bemused at this errand and obviously couldn’t wait to get back to bed, trailed by a very tall boy who turned out to be Tamms’s boyfriend, whom she had met once.

“How are you feeling?” I squeezed her arm.

She said, “OK,” and turned to look at a passenger being wheeled in a wheelchair. I figured she didn’t want to talk about it. She didn’t look like she had been crying, though. She clutched her little bag, which contained her laptop and the paraphernalia of a young lady, as we inched towards immigration.

Inside the plane, a surprise awaited us. For all her faults, sometimes Kenya Airways comes through in a big way, because when we got to the plane I realised that they had upgraded us to Business Class. Can you believe that? I didn’t ask for it. I didn’t think of it, seeing as it wasn’t a long-haul flight. I don’t know who did it, but it must have been Kanyingi Kuria from the communications office. A standup guy. He’ll never fully know how many points I scored by that one stroke of genius.

Because Tamms said, “You bought these seats!?”

“Hell no!” I said. “If I had that kind of money, I’d be sitting in the cockpit.”

She laughed.

I told her we had been upgraded. Then explained to her how that works. How sometimes the gods smile upon you, and someone sends you to the front seats. So we used our hot towels, and when the air hostess came around with refreshments, I told Tamms, “I think we should have champagne.”

She sniffed, pretentiously, piously. “It’s so early.”

“It’s not early,” I said. “It’s almost seven AM.”

Besides, I told her, you never know when you will ever fly Business Class again. It might be a very long, long time. Maybe when you are 28 and have a big job or a big business. “Besides, you go off to university for the first time only once.”

Champagne was brought in two glasses. The plane hummed around us, its engines a low, steady lullaby, while the morning light gathered beyond the windows. I raised my glass and, resisting any dad-speech, said simply, “To your good fortune.”

We touched glasses. She sipped and turned to look outside.

I wrote a text to Kanyingi, thanking him for making me look like a billion dollars.

We talked a bit. About my college days. How I lived in a shack, but how I loved that shack. About my very first roommate, Eddie Ogaro, how he bunked on top, drank a lot, read a lot, and slept on his bed under all his books. How his legs would dangle from the edges as he read out loud passages from whatever book he was reading. He fancied the Russian greats: Tolstoy, Pushkin and Gogol. But he also read Chinua Achebe and Wole. A lectiophile. We have remained in touch. How broke we were, but how happy we were. Young and free, and also foolish, because we didn’t know that we would never be those things again.

I was wistful, I will admit. The champagne.

I told her to do everything. To try everything apart from drugs. Not to ever say, “That is not for me.” Because you won’t know what’s not for you, not until you try it at least once.

To make friends.

I told her that because she is quiet and introverted, she will probably become very good friends with some very loud, short girl. And she won’t stand her the first time they meet. But they will be friends for life.

Have fun, I urged her. Study hard, but have all the fun. Open all doors, and leave them open.

We taxied off and then the plane settled above the cotton of clouds. She had breakfast like a savage; croissant and tea. I don’t know how people eat before 10am. What are you, a ruminant? I sipped my coffee.

She turned and said, “I think he had tears in his eyes.”

“Who, T?”

“Yeah.”

“Oh, that’s nice.” I said.

“Is it?”

“Yeah, nothing wrong with a man crying. I cry quite a bit.”

She said. “You do? You don’t strike me as someone who cries.”

“Oh, I do. Sometimes when I think of my mom I cry. Quite a bit, actually.”

She said that boys her age see crying as a weakness. “They say it’s not manly.”

“Boys your age don’t know what’s manly,” I said dryly.

She laughed and told me how, when she was young, her mom would point at the moon and tell her that was my mom. “So each time I see the moon, I think of your mom.”

I felt so many things when she said that, all of them gathered beneath the long shadow of grief for my dead mother. She would have fussed about her going away to university. She would have found a hundred things to worry about, and then worried about them all over again. And given her a long speech about being a woman of her own means.

We found a small studio in an apartment building terraced into the side of a hill. She lives alone. She will budget her own money. [OK, my money.] Build her own life. Make her own decisions.

People will ask if I felt sad or afraid of leaving her alone in another country. I felt neither. I felt proud and excited for her. She will grow into a formidable woman, because that is the stuff she is made of, like her aunts. She will find her way, her tribe, and she will thrive. She will also make mistakes and hopefully learn from them and she will be stronger for them. “This is your ship, not my ship,” I told her, “You get to steer it wherever you want to steer it. I’m only here to support you.”

OK, I’m a bit sad. Sad because she is no longer a child, and there is no way to get her back.
